title: Opportunity Solution Trees
intro: Map what you heard before choosing what to build.

learn.title: The structure
learn.text:
**Outcome** at the top.
**Opportunities** below it: needs, pain points and desires from interviews.
**Solutions** only under the target opportunity.
**Assumption tests** under each solution.

try.q: Where do solutions go on the tree?
options: Under every opportunity, so nothing is missed
try.explain: Brainstorming across the whole tree spreads the team thin.

learn.title: Disguised solutions
learn.text:
An opportunity can be addressed in **more than one way**. If there’s only one way, it’s a solution.

“I need a calendar export” → a solution.
“I need to see my schedule outside the app” → an opportunity.

Ask “why?” to find what’s underneath.

try.q: Which is an opportunity, not a solution?
options: I lose track of deadlines across projects
I need a Gantt chart view
Add email reminders for every upcoming project deadline
try.explain: It can be solved many ways.

learn.title: Parents, children, siblings
learn.text:
A **child is part of its parent.** Ask “what are other reasons why…?”
**Siblings are distinct:** you can address one without the others.
“Watch on a flight” and “watch on a train” share the parent “watch on the go”.

try.q: Why are “watch on a flight” and “watch on a train” siblings?
options: Their constraints differ under one parent
One is a solution to the other
They belong to two different outcomes on separate trees
try.explain: Offline viewing matters on planes; trains may have data.

learn.title: Choose a target
learn.text:
**Size:** how many, how often.
**Market position:** catch up or stand out.
**Strategic fit.**
**Customer importance** and satisfaction today.

**Leave effort out.** Compare one row at a time. It’s a two-way door.

try.q: Which factor should you leave out when choosing a target?
try.explain: Feasibility is tested later; judging it now rules out good options.

learn.title: Keep it alive
learn.text:
Before the first tree: a clear outcome and **three or four story interviews.**
Revisit **every 3–4 interviews.**
Still messy after **6–8**? Check how you interview.
New tree only when the outcome **changes direction.**

try.q: When do you start a new tree?
options: Every quarter, together with the planning cycle
try.explain: A new number for the same outcome keeps the same tree.

options: The support ticket queue on its own, sorted by volume
test.explain: Tickets and analytics suggest what to ask about; they aren’t opportunities on their own.

test.q: How many solutions should you compare for a target?
test.explain: Comparing stops the team defending its first idea.

test.q: Why avoid scoring formulas for opportunities?
options: Numbers make judgements look like facts
They take far too long to calculate for every opportunity
test.explain: It discourages revisiting a wrong call.

options: One row of the tree at a time
All of them in one ranked list
By how quickly they can ship
test.explain: Compare like with like, then go deeper within the winner.

test.q: Which is a common tree mistake?
options: One tree for the whole company
A tree with only one outcome
test.explain: A company-wide view needs a KPI tree or an experience map instead.

test.q: What is needed before the first tree?
options: An outcome and three or four story interviews
Formal approval from every stakeholder involved in the product
test.explain: Without stories, the opportunities are invented.
